description: The Tauri IPC surface for StackVo Desktop — contract v1. Derived 1:1 from the Express routes in core/ui/server/routes/ and the Socket.io events in core/ui/server/, plus the commands the desktop app needs that no HTTP endpoint ever provided. This file is the agreement between the Vue front end and the Rust core; both sides are generated/checked against it.

conventions.naming: snake_case, <domain>_<verb>. The same string is the Rust #[tauri::command] fn name and the JS invoke() key.

envelope.before: Express returned { success, data?, message?, meta? } and the axios interceptor unwrapped .data — a 200 with success:false was treated as an error.
envelope.after: Tauri commands return Result<T, StackvoError>. Ok(T) is the payload directly (no envelope). Err(e) rejects the invoke() promise. The success:false-with-HTTP-200 ambiguity disappears.
envelope.migration: client/src/lib/api.js is the ONLY file that changes: its interceptor logic becomes a thin invoke() wrapper that re-throws StackvoError as an Error with .code and .hint attached. Pinia stores are untouched.

conventions.argCasing: Rust params are snake_case; Tauri auto-converts camelCase from JS. Send snake_case explicitly to avoid ambiguity.
conventions.longRunning: Any operation that can exceed ~2s (build, compose up, image pull) MUST NOT block on its return value. It returns an OperationId immediately and reports progress via events. This replaces the 600s nginx proxy timeout hack.
conventions.idempotency: start/stop/restart on an already-in-that-state container succeed silently (matches current DockerService behaviour).

codes.ENGINE_UNREACHABLE: Docker daemon not running or socket/pipe not accessible. Replaces the ECONNREFUSED stack spam that isDockerUnreachable() papered over. The UI MUST offer engine_start().
codes.NOT_FOUND: Container, project or service does not exist.
codes.INVALID_INPUT: Failed schema validation. `details` carries the field path.
codes.INVALID_MANIFEST: stackvo.json exists but violates project.schema.json. `details.path` names the offending key.
codes.UNSUPPORTED: Requested runtime/extension/server/platform feature has no implementation in v1 (e.g. runtime=python, extension=pdo_oci, external terminal off macOS).
codes.GENERATE_FAILED: The generator ran and failed. `details.log` carries stderr.
codes.BUILD_FAILED: Docker build returned non-zero. `details.log_path` points at logs/build/<service>.log.
codes.CONFLICT: Port or domain already claimed by another project.
codes.NO_WORKSPACE: No StackVo directory is selected, or the selected one no longer looks like a StackVo checkout. Desktop-only: the web UI could never hit this because it was mounted inside the repo it managed. The UI MUST offer workspace_pick().

errors.policy: No error message may contain a raw shell command line or a value matching the secret redaction regex from env.schema.json.

engine_status.why: There was NO endpoint for this. The web UI could not report a stopped Docker daemon because the UI itself was a container that could not start. This is the single most important new command — it is what makes the desktop app usable when Docker is down.
engine_status.polling: Called on startup and on a 5s timer while disconnected; emits engine:status_changed on transition.

engine_start.why: Launch Docker Desktop (macOS/Windows) or `systemctl --user start docker` (Linux). Resolves the chicken-and-egg problem end to end.
engine_start.notes: Best-effort. Returns Ok as soon as the launch is issued; the caller waits on engine:status_changed.

preflight.why: Everything that has to be true before the app can do anything: a checkout, a reachable daemon, compose v2, the shared network, a projects directory, bash, and mkcert. Without it the app opened regardless and each button failed on its own terms — three different errors, one cause each, none stated up front.
preflight.notes: Runs before the first screen. `Unknown` is a distinct state from failure: with the engine down there is no answer to "does the network exist", and reporting one sends the user after the wrong problem. Declared retroactively — this shipped without a contract entry.

preflight_fix.why: A requirement that reports a problem the app could have fixed itself is a diagnosis pretending to be a product. `fixable` on each Requirement says which ids this accepts.
preflight_fix.notes: Rejects any id it cannot fix rather than silently succeeding — a no-op that returns Ok would report the requirement as repaired on the next poll and it would still be broken. Accepts 'network', 'projects' and 'engine'; the UI reaches engine start through engine_start (it polls for the daemon coming up), the 'engine' arm here is for headless callers. Declared retroactively.

doctor.why: The boot gate answers "can the app run"; this answers the failures that arrive later, one failed compose up at a time. The single most common one — a host port already taken — compose reports as "address already in use" with no word on by what. The doctor names the culprit: the stack's own container (fine), someone else's container (named), or a host process (named, with pid).
doctor.notes: Diagnosis only. Every repair stays behind its own command — preflight_fix, hosts_apply (behind its reviewed diff), generate_run, docker_prune — so no confirmation flow is bypassed. Degrades honestly: no workspace ⇒ port and generated checks read unknown; engine down ⇒ space is null and port owners cannot be named.

docker_disk_usage.why: docker_system_resources reports totals; the question a full disk raises is *which project*. Every StackVo container with its image size and writable layer, plus stack-built images whose container is gone — the bytes nobody remembers spending. No native-binary competitor can ship this at all.
docker_disk_usage.notes: imageDedicated separates images this stack built (stackvo-<name>, freed by removing the member) from shared upstream images (mysql:8.0, freed by nothing short of docker rmi). Sorted largest first.

tunnel_status.why: Webhook testing (Stripe, GitHub) had no answer: myapp.loc does not exist on the internet. This reports every running tunnel sidecar and its assigned public URL.
tunnel_status.notes: The URL is read from the sidecar's own log on every call rather than cached — what the log says is what is actually live, across app restarts and container crashes alike. `url` is null while cloudflared is still connecting; the UI polls until it appears.

tunnel_start.why: Starts a cloudflared quick-tunnel sidecar on the stack's network, forwarding a random trycloudflare.com URL to the project's container. No account, no token — and no host-binary competitor can attach to the container network at all.
tunnel_start.notes: An operation because the first start pulls the cloudflared image, which can take minutes. Targets the project container directly (with the local domain as Host header): with SSL on, every Traefik project router is websecure-only, which a public visitor cannot handshake against. Refuses when the project container is not running — a tunnel serving 502s looks like it worked. The URL that results is public and unauthenticated while the tunnel runs; the UI says so.

tunnel_stop.notes: The sidecar runs with --rm, so stop is also removal — nothing is left behind to leak the old URL.

project_scaffold.why: The create half of P0-1 (detection/adoption shipped first). Runs the framework's own installer in a throwaway container — composer create-project, wp-cli, create-next-app — so nothing is installed on the host and only the bind-mounted project directory survives.
project_scaffold.notes: Ends where adoption begins: the UI follows with project_adopt, which detects runtime/server/document root from what the installer actually wrote — the same machinery as a git clone. Every installer command is pinned non-interactive (a prompt inside an operation console is a hang, not a question). On unix runs --user uid:gid so files land owned by the user, not root. Refuses a non-empty directory; a failed install that wrote nothing removes the husk so the retry is not blocked.

worker_options.why: Which workers this project can offer, from its files alone: artisan offers 'queue' and 'scheduler', laravel/horizon in composer.json adds 'horizon'. A Node project gets an empty list, not an error.

worker_status.why: A Laravel app runs queue:work, the scheduler and Horizon beside the web server; locally they live in a forgotten terminal tab, which is why "my job never ran" is a support staple. This reports every worker sidecar with its restart count — the self-heal made visible; a large number is a crash loop, not a success story.

worker_start.notes: The sidecar runs the project's own image (same PHP, extensions, bind mount and network, so .env and the database resolve as the web container sees them) with --restart unless-stopped — self-healing is Docker's own supervisor, not reimplemented. queue:work carries --max-time=3600 on purpose: a worker holds the code it booted with, and an hour caps how long it serves yesterday's code. Refuses when the project has no built container.

worker_stop.notes: Removal, not just stop: with unless-stopped, a merely-stopped container is one engine restart away from coming back.

docker_prune.why: SystemResources has reported reclaimable bytes since Phase 1 with no way to act on the number. Dangling images accumulate on every rebuild, and this app rebuilds a lot — every Xdebug toggle, every extension change.
docker_prune.notes: Images means dangling images only (the engine's default prune set — rebuildable by definition). Volumes are a separate flag because the engine's "unused" means "not currently mounted", and the database of a stopped project qualifies; the UI warns before passing volumes:true. Guarded by the 'prune' inflight subject.

workspace_get.why: The web UI never needed this — it ran inside the StackVo repo, so its root was `/app` by mount. A desktop app has to be told, or work it out. Returns the resolved root plus how it was resolved, so the UI can show the user which checkout it is driving.

workspace_set.notes: Validates that the path contains core/cli/stackvo.sh and projects/ before accepting it, then persists it. Rejects with NO_WORKSPACE and an explanation rather than silently accepting a wrong folder.

workspace_pick.notes: Opens the native directory picker, then applies workspace_set. Returns null if the user cancels.

project_get.why: ProjectDetail.vue currently re-fetches the whole list and filters client-side.

project_validate.why: Pre-flight the new-project form against project.schema.json + php-extensions.json before anything touches disk. Today a bad extension name is only discovered when the Docker build fails minutes later.

project_create.notes: Writes the manifest, runs generate, then builds. The build half is what makes it an operation rather than a mutation.

project_delete.notes: remove_files is NEW and MUST default to false. The current deleteProject() removes the project directory outright with no confirmation contract — a desktop app deleting user source code needs an explicit opt-in.

project_manifest_write.why: Editing an existing project is impossible today — the UI can only create and delete. MUST honour the write rules in project.schema.json (extensions last, one runtime block).

service_enable.notes: Flips SERVICE_<NAME>_ENABLE in .env, regenerates, then brings the profile up.

service_dependencies.notes: Kept for completeness; services_list already returns required/optional/unmetDependencies per service, so the front end has no reason to call this separately.

host_stats.v1Change: Backed by the `sysinfo` crate on the host instead of reading /proc from inside a container. The 293-line HostStatsService with its macOS fallbacks collapses to a direct, correct read — this is the clearest early win of the port.

container_stats_history.notes: Sampler runs at 60s (startStatsSampler). v1 MUST persist history across app restarts — today it lives in memory and dies with the container.

container_logs_open.why: Log following existed only as `stackvo logs` in the CLI. The UI had no way to tail a container.

app_logs.why: The container stream carries stdout and stderr, which is what the entrypoint and the web server say — not what the application records. A Laravel exception goes to storage/logs/laravel.log, an nginx 502 to the mounted error.log, and a queue worker that died to its own file under supervisord. None of those reach stdout, so none of them were visible anywhere in the app.
app_logs.notes: Reads the host filesystem, not the container: the generated compose mounts projects/<name> at /var/www/html and logs/projects/<name> at /var/log, so both roots are already there. No engine required — which is the point, because a container that crashed on boot is exactly when its log is worth reading and exactly when there is nothing left to exec into. Discovery recurses, because Laravel channels nest (storage/logs/parser/parser-2026-07-28.log is a real path from the checkout this was built against), and is capped at depth 3 and 60 files so a stray node_modules cannot turn it into a full-disk walk.

app_log_open.why: Follows one of those files. Shares the event pair with container_logs_open because the viewer renders one kind of line; a second pair would have meant a second frontend listener free to drift from the first. Closed with container_logs_close — one registry of abort handles, one way to stop a stream.
app_log_open.notes: `id` is an opaque `app:` or `server:` handle from app_logs, never a path. Paths do not cross the boundary in either direction: a log viewer that accepts an absolute path from its own frontend is a file reader for the whole disk. The id's components are checked for traversal before the filesystem is touched, and the resolved path is checked against its root again afterwards, because a symlink inside the project can escape with no `..` in sight. Polled twice a second rather than watched — a notification still only says that something changed, so the read-the-delta path exists either way. A file shorter than the reader's offset was truncated or rotated (`> laravel.log`, or a daily channel rolling over) and restarts from the top instead of going silent for ever.

env_get.notes: MUST redact secret-matching keys unless `reveal: true` is passed and the user has confirmed in-session.

env_reveal.why: env_get redacts secrets, so revealing one needs a separate call the user has to ask for. Returning the whole map unmasked on a flag would put every password in one payload the moment anyone wanted to see one.
env_reveal.notes: One key per call, by design. Declared retroactively: this shipped in lib.rs without a contract entry and suite E was reporting it as UNDECLARED_COMMAND.

env_set.why: Settings.vue is a 24-line stub because .env was read-only over HTTP. Writing MUST preserve comments, key order and blank lines — a naive rewrite destroys a 159-key hand-annotated file.

catalog_get.v1Change: Served from the bundled contracts (php-extensions.json + env.schema.json), no longer re-parsed out of .env on every request. Runtimes without generators are marked available:false rather than silently offered.

generate_run.why: `stackvo generate` was only ever invoked as a side effect of project_create / service_enable, via execAsync on a shell string. Making it a first-class command is what lets the fs-watcher regenerate automatically.

compose_down.why: `stackvo down` existed only in the CLI — the web UI could never stop the stack, because doing so would have killed the UI itself.

pty_open.v1Change: PtyTarget is NEW: { kind: 'container', name } or { kind: 'host', cwd }. node-pty could only reach containers because it ran inside one; portable-pty on the host can open a real host shell in the project directory.

terminal_open_external.v1Change: Always works. The HTTP version returned HTTP 400 with 'Terminal cannot be opened from containerized environment' — it could never succeed in the shipped configuration.

hosts_status.why: readHostsFile() could only READ a read-only mount and report isDomainConfigured. Same capability, but now it feeds a fix action.
hosts_status.notes: Rust-internal: projects_list uses it to fill `domainConfigured`. Deliberately not wrapped for JS — the list payload already carries the answer, and a second round trip is a way for the two to disagree.

hosts_apply.why: Removes the manual `sudo tee -a /etc/hosts` step from the README. MUST show a diff and require explicit confirmation before elevating; MUST back up the file; MUST only touch lines inside a StackVo-managed marker block.
hosts_apply.notes: Writes the previewed text via the OS elevation prompt (osascript / pkexec / UAC). Only lines inside the `# >>> stackvo >>>` marker block are rewritten; everything else in the file is byte-identical. A cancelled prompt is PERMISSION_DENIED, not a crash.

open_path.notes: Implemented in the front end via the opener plugin rather than as a Rust command: the plugin already does exactly this, and wrapping it would add a hop with no behaviour of its own. The capability is allow-listed in capabilities/default.json.

open_url.notes: Same as open_path. The plugin restricts schemes; the allow-list in capabilities/default.json is the control point.

open_in_editor.notes: Editor command from preferences; default: detect VS Code, fall back to the OS handler.

pick_directory.why: Adopting an existing folder as a project is impossible today; paths are typed by hand.
pick_directory.notes: Used directly by the front end. `workspace_pick` is the Rust command that matters, because it pairs the picker with validation and persistence.

apps_available.notes: Terminals and editors present on this machine, each with { id, name, icon, available }. Entries that are not installed are returned with available:false rather than omitted, so the picker can grey them out — a list that silently drops them reads as lack of support.

window_close_action.notes: Carries out the choice the close dialog collected, optionally storing it as closeBehaviour. Four behaviours exist including "ask"; the extra "quit" (close, leave the stack running) is meaningful here because the containers are Docker's and outlive the app.

tray_relabel.notes: Re-label the tray menu after the user changes language. The tray is built natively and has six strings of its own; without this it keeps the language it was built with until the next launch.

logs_info.returns: { directory: string|null, newestFile: string|null, totalBytes: number }
logs_info.notes: Where the diagnostic log lives. New to the desktop app — the container UI wrote to stdout, which docker logs captured and nobody kept. The path differs per platform (~/Library/Logs on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA% on Windows, ~/.local/share on Linux) and none is somewhere a user would look unprompted.

updater_status.returns: { configured: boolean, hasPublicKey: boolean, endpoints: number }
updater_status.notes: Whether this build can verify an update. Tauri checks a bundle's signature against the public key compiled into the app; with an empty `pubkey` every check fails inside the plugin with a message about signatures, which reads like a server fault and is a build fault. Read from tauri.conf.json via include_str! so the answer describes the binary, not the working tree.

system_accent.returns: { available: boolean, name: string|null, hex: string|null }
system_accent.why: The desktop's own accent colour, so the app can match it instead of shipping a brand colour that clashes with everyone's system theme.
system_accent.notes: macOS reads AppleHighlightColor via `defaults` and maps it to the eight colours the OS itself draws with. Elsewhere `available` is false and both fields are null — Windows keeps its accent in the registry, and saying "unknown" beats returning a wrong blue. Declared retroactively — this shipped without a contract entry.

prefs_get.notes: Replaces the localStorage-backed usePreferences composable with the Tauri store plugin.

updates_check.notes: Needs tauri-plugin-updater plus a signing key and a release endpoint — i.e. a release pipeline, not just code. Deferred to Phase 4 alongside signed builds. Declared here so the surface is complete and the gap is visible.

hosts_plan.why: Computes the exact replacement text WITHOUT elevating, so the UI can show a diff and ask first. Elevating and explaining afterwards would be the wrong order for the one operation that touches a system file.

hosts_missing.why: Every project domain with no hosts entry. Drives the one-click fix; the web UI could detect this but had no way to act on it.

cert_status.why: HTTPS was already working and entirely invisible. `core/cli/utils/generate-ssl-certs.sh` issues an mkcert wildcard covering stackvo.loc and every project domain, and traefik.sh installs it as the default certificate — but nothing in the app could say whether mkcert was installed, whether the CA was trusted, whether the certificate had expired, or which domains it actually covered. A user whose new project shows a browser warning had no way to learn why.
cert_status.notes: Reads only: it never runs mkcert and never writes. The SAN list and expiry are parsed out of the certificate itself rather than inferred from the project list, because the file on disk is what the browser validates against — a list of what SHOULD be covered would agree with the certificate right up until it mattered.

cert_plan.why: Same order as hosts_plan: say what would change before doing it. Reissuing replaces the file Traefik is serving, and `installCa` can touch the system trust store, so neither should be the first thing the user learns about it.
cert_plan.notes: `domains` is the exact argument list mkcert would be invoked with — the same value cert_apply uses, not a second computation that could differ.

cert_apply.why: Reissues the wildcard certificate for the domains the projects actually have, and — when the CA is not trusted yet — installs it. Without this the certificate goes stale the moment a project is created, and on Linux and Windows the CA is never trusted at all: the Bash helper's trust step returns early on anything but macOS, so those users get a browser warning and no explanation.
cert_apply.notes: Trust installation delegates to `mkcert -install` rather than reimplementing four trust stores (macOS keychain, Linux ca-certificates, NSS for Firefox and Chrome, Windows Root). mkcert may need a password for the system store; on Linux it shells out to sudo, which a GUI process has no terminal for. That failure MUST be reported with the exact command to run, not swallowed — a CA that silently failed to install looks identical to one that worked until the browser disagrees. Issuing the certificate itself writes only inside the workspace and never elevates.

project_adoptable.why: `project_create` refuses when the directory already exists, so a folder cloned into projects/ could not be brought under management at all — the only way in was writing stackvo.json by hand. On the checkout this was written against, 11 of 21 directories under projects/ were in that state: real code, unmanaged.
project_adoptable.notes: Reads only, and needs no Docker. Each entry carries a detected runtime, server, document root and framework, plus the files that detection was based on — a document root inferred wrongly produces a project that builds, starts and serves a 404, which is a failure with no error attached to it.

args.name: string
args.spec: ProjectSpec (optional — defaults to what was detected)

project_adopt.why: Writes stackvo.json for a directory that is already there, then regenerates. The counterpart of project_create, which requires the directory to be absent.
project_adopt.notes: Refuses when a manifest already exists — adopting a managed project would silently overwrite settings the user chose. The spec is validated against project.schema.json exactly as project_create's is; detection fills the form, it does not bypass the check.

mail_status.why: StackVo has shipped a mail catcher all along and never showed it — reading a captured message meant leaving for a browser tab, which is exactly the round trip four competitors charge for removing.
mail_status.notes: Reads both MailHog and Mailpit. The upstream template installs the unmaintained `mailhog/mailhog`; Mailpit is what the ecosystem moved to, and swapping renames a service, its .env keys, its container and its volume — a migration for every running stack. Supporting both is the same stance the app takes everywhere else: it manages a checkout, it does not dictate one. `error` is set when the container is up but its API did not answer, because that otherwise renders as an empty inbox, which is a lie.

mail_messages.notes: Both wire formats are normalised in Rust. They agree on almost nothing: MailHog spells an address as `{Mailbox, Domain}` and buries the subject in a header array, Mailpit uses `{Name, Address}` and a field. Reading either as the other yields an inbox of blank rows that still look like messages.

mail_message.notes: Mailpit returns decoded text and HTML parts. MailHog returns the raw MIME document and leaves decoding to the caller, so `html` is always null there — showing a half-decoded multipart as if it were the message would be worse than showing the source.

mail_clear.notes: DESTRUCTIVE in the small: it empties the inbox. The UI MUST confirm, but this needs no backup — a mail catcher is a bin by design.

db_targets.why: Which database services can be dumped, what they are called, and whether they are running. The credentials were already read out of .env and rendered in the services list; what was missing was anything to do with them.
db_targets.notes: Reads .env and the engine. A service that is enabled but not running is still listed, with `running: false` — the reason a dump cannot start right now is worth showing next to the button that is disabled because of it.

db_dump.why: Lerd sells snapshots, Laragon sells automatic backups, ServBay sells both; StackVo had no way to take a copy of a database at all. The tools are already inside the container — `mysqldump`, `pg_dump` and `mongodump` ship with the images the stack runs.
db_dump.notes: Streams the dump straight from `docker exec` into the chosen file rather than buffering it: a production-sized database does not fit in a UI process's memory, and the failure would arrive as an out-of-memory kill with no explanation. The password is passed through the child's environment and named — not valued — on the docker command line, so it does not appear in `ps` output on a shared machine.

db_restore.why: A backup nobody has restored is a file, not a backup.
db_restore.notes: DESTRUCTIVE: this replaces the contents of the target database. The UI MUST name the database and require confirmation before calling it. Reads the file into the container's stdin, the mirror of how the dump was written.

xdebug_status.why: Step debugging is the thing Docker makes hardest and the thing a PHP developer needs most. `xdebug` was already in the extension catalog with per-version pecl pins, so it could be compiled in by hand-editing stackvo.json — and then it still would not connect, because nothing set xdebug.mode or told it which host the IDE is on. This reports all three layers separately: listed in the manifest, present in the built image, and live in the running container.
xdebug_status.notes: `active` is read from the running container's environment rather than assumed from the manifest. The two disagree in a case users hit: `stackvo up` from the CLI does not layer the overlay this app writes, so it recreates the container without the Xdebug environment and debugging stops working with nothing on screen to explain it.

xdebug_set.why: One switch instead of three manual steps: adding the extension to the manifest, configuring the client host and port, and telling the IDE where the code is mounted.
xdebug_set.notes: Writes `php.extensions` in the manifest and re-renders `generated/docker-compose.xdebug.yml`. The extension is COMPILED IN, so enabling it needs a rebuild before it takes effect — `needsRebuild` says so rather than letting the toggle look finished. Writing the manifest canonicalises it the same way project_manifest_write does (`webserver` becomes `server`); that is the contract's rule for writers, not a side effect of this command.

project_dockerfile_preview.why: Runs the Rust generator port alongside the Bash one so its output can be compared before it replaces anything. `matchesBashOutput` is the differential check, live against the user's own projects rather than only against fixtures.
project_dockerfile_preview.notes: Strict mode is the behaviour change made visible: where Bash silently drops an incompatible extension, this refuses and names it. `skipped` always reports what compat mode would have dropped, so the difference is legible either way.

generator_verify.why: The migration gate. A fixture suite only covers the cases someone thought to write down; this renders every generated file with the Rust port against the user's real projects and real .env, so a divergence surfaces on their machine before anything depends on it.
generator_verify.notes: Reads only — it never writes a generated file. `readyToTakeOver` is true when every file matches byte-for-byte.

generate_with.why: The staged handover. The generator's output is the input to every container the user runs, so 'probably identical' is not a standard worth shipping. Bash runs in every mode; `rust` refuses to write when the two disagree, so the switch cannot silently change anyone's images.
generate_with.notes: `verify` is the mode to leave on during the transition: Bash still writes, and any divergence is reported without being acted on. Replaces generate_run, which is kept for callers that only ever want Bash.

events._note: Names are preserved from Socket.io so the Vue listeners keep working, with ONE deliberate change: the terminal events move from dash to colon separators for consistency. That is a 4-line change in the terminal component.

app:close_requested.notes: The window was asked to close and closeBehaviour is "ask". Rust prevents the close and emits this; the front end shows the choice dialog and answers with window_close_action.

build:built.note: The IMAGE finished building. `project_build` has three stages — generate, build image, recreate container — and this marks the end of the second. The UI shows 'starting container…' between this and build:success.

build:success.note: The container is up from the fresh image; the whole operation is done.

compose:progress.why: `docker compose up/down` writes its progress to stderr line by line. The old UI held the HTTP request open for the whole run (proxy_read_timeout 600s) and showed nothing until it ended.

scaffold:progress.why: composer create-project downloads a framework — minutes on a slow line, and the installer's own lines are the only honest progress there is.

tunnel:progress.why: The first tunnel_start pulls the cloudflared image; the pull's own lines belong in the operation console like every other long-running docker invocation.

engine:status_changed.why: Drives the whole-app connected/disconnected state and the tray icon.

container:state_changed.why: Sourced from the Docker events stream. Today the UI polls on a visibility-gated timer (useVisiblePolling); a push stream removes the polling entirely.

manifest:changed.why: fs-watcher on projects/*/stackvo.json. Enables 'config changed — regenerate?' instead of the user remembering to run `stackvo generate`.
manifest:changed.notes: Debounced 400ms — editors write a file several times per save. The app does NOT regenerate on its own; it offers the action, because rebuilding a container under someone who is mid-edit is worse than the staleness it fixes.

hosts:changed.why: Warn when a project's domain has no hosts entry, with a one-click fix.

db:progress.notes: The tools write progress and warnings to stderr; stdout is the dump itself and never reaches the UI.

xdebug:changed.why: The toggle changes the manifest and the compose overlay, so anything showing the project's configuration or its pending-regenerate state is now out of date.

certs:changed.why: The certificate was reissued, so anything showing coverage or an expiry has to re-read it. Traefik picks the new file up on its own; the UI has no way to know without being told.

_removed.generate:error: Removed: `generate:done` carries `success` and `error`, and generate_run returns Err as well. A second failure channel is one more thing to keep consistent for no gain.
_removed.terminal:error: Removed: pty_open returns Err when the shell cannot start, which is the only case this covered.

Workspace.note: root is null when source is 'none'. `source` exists so the UI can say WHY it is pointing at a given checkout — silently guessing wrong would be worse than asking.

ProjectSpec.note: The create form's payload IS a project manifest. The old POST body used a flat shape (runtime, version, extensions at top level) that ProjectService then reassembled — and reassembled wrongly for node. v1 sends the manifest itself, so there is nothing to reassemble.

Project.name: string
Project.note: manifest_valid/manifest_errors are NEW: an invalid manifest must be visible in the list, not a silently missing project.

Doctor.note: ports.requiredBy is the compose service that publishes the port, read from the generated files — which is the enabled set, because the generator only writes enabled services. ports.state: ok = free or held by the stack itself; warn = a docker backend holds it but the engine could not say whose container; fail = a named conflict. generated.state: warn = an input (.env or a manifest) is newer than the oldest generated compose file, detail names it; fail = never generated.

ProgressEvent.subject: string
ProgressEvent.note: One line of a running process's merged stdout+stderr. Merged deliberately: docker compose writes progress to stderr and results to stdout, and separating them makes the log read out of order.

FinishedEvent.subject: string
FinishedEvent.note: On failure `error` carries the last few output lines rather than a generic exit-code message — that tail is almost always the real cause.

HostsPlan.note: `preview` is the exact text that will be written — the same value the diff is rendered from, so what the user approves is what lands.

CertStatus.note: `covered` is read from the certificate's subjectAltName, not from the project list. `missing` is wildcard-aware: `*.stackvo.loc` covers `api.stackvo.loc` but not `shop.loc` and not `a.b.stackvo.loc`, because a wildcard matches exactly one label. `ca_trusted` is null when the platform gives no cheap way to ask, which is not the same as false. `stale` is true when anything is missing or the certificate has expired — it is what the UI badges.

LogFile.label: string
LogFile.note: `id` is `<root>:<relative path>` — `app:` for files the code wrote under projects/<name>, `server:` for files the stack wrote under logs/projects/<name>. It is a handle, not a path: it is what app_log_open takes, and it is the reason no absolute path is ever accepted from the frontend. `modified` is epoch seconds so the date is formatted in the user's locale rather than the backend's.

CertPlan.note: `domains` is the exact SAN list mkcert will be invoked with, so what the user approves is what lands — the same relationship `preview` has to the hosts file. `remove` names domains the certificate still covers that no project asks for any more; they disappear on the next reissue and are listed so that is not a surprise. `rejected` names domains dropped as invalid rather than silently omitting them.
CertPlan.reloadedNote: Writing the certificate is not enough to change what a browser gets. Traefik's file provider watches generated/traefik/dynamic, and the certificates are not in it — routes.yml only points at them, and a certFile is read while the dynamic configuration is parsed. So cert_apply rewrites the watched files with their own bytes to force a reparse. Observed on a real checkout: Traefik up two days, serving a certificate a day older than the one on disk. False after an apply means the new certificate is on disk but not yet served.

Detected.note: `evidence` names the files the answer was read from, and `confidence` says how much to trust it. `guess` means nothing recognisable was there and the fields are defaults the user is expected to correct — presenting that as an answer is the failure this distinction exists to avoid.

Adoptable.name: string
Adoptable.note: `has_files` ignores dotfiles: a directory holding nothing but a `.DS_Store` is empty for this purpose, and offering it for adoption as if it had code in it is how a real checkout looked before this was handled.

MailStatus.note: `unread` is null rather than 0 on MailHog, which has no concept of a read message — a zero would render as "all caught up" on a server that cannot know. `available` is false when the checkout has neither catcher at all, which is different from having one that is switched off.

MailMessage.subject: string
MailMessage.note: `date` is passed through unparsed: the UI formats it in the user's locale, and the two servers disagree about which field it lives in, not about the format. `snippet` is null on MailHog, which does not send one — deriving it from the raw body would render MIME boundaries as preview text.

DbTarget.note: `extension` is the suggested file extension, and it differs by engine rather than being cosmetic: mysql and postgres dump to plain SQL a person can read and edit, while mongodump produces a gzipped BSON archive that only mongorestore can read. `database` is null for mongo, where the dump covers the whole server.

XdebugStatus.note: Three layers, deliberately not collapsed into one boolean. `enabled` is what the manifest asks for; `needsRebuild` is true while the image predates that ask, because extensions are compiled in and a toggle that looked done but changed nothing would be worse than no toggle; `active` is what the running container actually carries, and is null when there is no container to read. `hostPath` and `containerPath` are the two halves of the IDE's path mapping — the mapping is the step people get wrong, and both sides are already known here.

Preflight.note: `detail` is what the machine said — a version, a path, the daemon's own error — and is deliberately not translated. `ready` ignores warnings: mkcert reports `warn` rather than `fail` because a stack without HTTPS still runs, it just serves a browser warning.

DockerfilePreview.skipped: [{extension, reason}] — what the Bash generator drops without telling anyone

GeneratorReport.warnings: string[] — configuration problems the port can see and StackVo does not report, e.g. C-20

unreachableRemoved: POST /api/terminal/:c/open returned HTTP 400 unconditionally in the shipped container configuration — replaced by terminal_open_external, which works.
coverage.phase3: Tray, notifications, fs-watcher, hosts helper, PTY, autostart and single-instance. The hosts helper replaces the README's manual `sudo tee -a /etc/hosts` step; the PTY replaces a terminal endpoint that returned HTTP 400 unconditionally in the shipped container configuration.
coverage.implementationStatus: Suite E of tools/validate-contracts.mjs cross-checks this file against the Rust registry in src-tauri/src/lib.rs and the JS wrappers in src/lib/ipc.js. A command declared here but not registered shows up as a NOT_IMPLEMENTED warning, so this list cannot quietly drift ahead of the code.
